title: The K-Pg Extinction Event
keyIdea: About 66 million years ago, at the end of the Cretaceous period, an asteroid about 10 km wide hit Earth. It made the Chicxulub crater, about 180 km wide, now buried under the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico. Dust, soot and sulfur blocked sunlight, so plants died back and food chains broke. About three quarters of all species died out, including every dinosaur except the birds. The evidence includes a thin clay layer found round the world, rich in iridium (a metal common in asteroids but rare in Earth's crust), with shocked quartz and glass beads, and dinosaur fossils only below it.
familyTip: Stack a few slices of different bread or coloured play dough to make rock layers, and push a toy dinosaur into a low layer. Ask which layer went down first and which is oldest. Then look at a world map together and find the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico, where the crater is buried. If you have a garden bird feeder, talk about how the birds visiting it are living dinosaurs.

visual.caption: Did each group die out or live on after the K-Pg extinction? Drag each card, or tap it and then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: dig to where dinosaur fossils stop, probe for iridium, match the crater, order the food-chain collapse, sort survivors and build one.

kid: Rock forms in layers, one on top of another. So the deepest layers are the oldest. In cliffs from the end of the age of dinosaurs, there are dinosaur bones in the low layers. Then there is a thin layer of clay. Above it, there are no dinosaur bones at all. Something big happened at that line, 66 million years ago.

In 1980, Luis Alvarez and his son Walter tested that clay in Italy. It held about 30 times more iridium than the rock around it. Iridium is a metal that is rare in Earth's rocks but common in asteroids. They said a huge asteroid must have hit Earth. Later, a crater about 180 km wide was found under the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico. It is called Chicxulub, and it is 66 million years old.

The asteroid was about 10 km wide. It threw hot rock into the sky and started fires. Dust, soot and sulfur blocked the Sun for months or years. It got dark and cold. Plants could not make food, so plant-eaters starved, and then the meat-eaters did too.

About three out of every four kinds of living things died out. All the big dinosaurs went, and so did pterosaurs, mosasaurs and ammonites. Small animals that ate seeds, insects or dead things did best. Birds lived on, and birds are dinosaurs. So are the pigeons and robins you see today.
adult: Ages 9 to 11. This fits Key Stage 2 science in the National Curriculum in England (Year 3 rocks and fossils; Year 6 evolution and inheritance: fossils give information about living things from millions of years ago) and NGSS 4-ESS1-1 (patterns in rock layers and fossils show changes over time) and 3-LS4-1 (fossils show organisms and environments of long ago). Key words: extinction, mass extinction, fossil, rock layer (stratum), sedimentary rock, Cretaceous, Palaeogene, asteroid, impact crater, iridium, evidence, food chain, producer, consumer.

The lab has six tasks. Children dig down a cliff like those at Hell Creek, Montana, and find the thin clay where dinosaur fossils stop. They move a probe through the layers and find the iridium spike in the clay (about 30 times background, as at Gubbio). They drop the asteroid on the crater that fits by age and size: Chicxulub, not Meteor Crater (1.2 km, 50,000 years) or Manicouagan (214 million years). They put the impact-winter chain in order, sort eight groups into died out and survived, and build an animal with survivor traits.

Common mistakes. Many children think the asteroid hit every dinosaur directly; most died later, when food chains collapsed. Others think no dinosaurs survived, but birds are living dinosaurs, while pterosaurs (which died out) were flying reptiles, not dinosaurs. Children also mix up the order of layers (the top is youngest) and think dinosaurs and early humans lived together. Be careful with 'all life died': about three quarters of species died out, so a quarter survived. Huge volcanic eruptions in India (the Deccan Traps) happened around the same time, and scientists still discuss how much they added.

practice.prompt: In a cliff, dinosaur bones are found in the layers below a thin clay layer but never above it. What does that tell us?
choices: Dinosaurs died out around the time the clay layer formed
Dinosaurs lived after the clay layer formed
The clay layer is the oldest rock in the cliff
practice.hint: Lower layers are older. Where do the dinosaur bones stop?
practice.explain: Layers below the clay are older and have dinosaurs; layers above are younger and have none. So the dinosaurs died out when the clay formed.

practice.prompt: A rock has {r} units of iridium. The boundary clay has 30 times as much. How many units does the clay have?
practice.hint: Times as much means multiply. Work out {r} × 30.
practice.explain: {r} × 30 = {=30*r} units. A jump that big in one thin layer is what pointed scientists to an asteroid.

practice.prompt: A dinosaur bone comes from a layer {a} million years old. The K-Pg clay layer is 66 million years old. How many million years before the extinction did this dinosaur live?
practice.hint: Older layers have bigger ages. Take 66 away from {a}.
practice.explain: {a} − 66 = {=a-66}, so it lived {=a-66} million years before the extinction. Its layer sits lower in the cliff than the clay.

practice.prompt: Why did Triceratops die out, even though the asteroid hit far away in Mexico?
choices: Dust and soot blocked the Sun, so the plants it ate died back
The asteroid landed right on every Triceratops
It was too slow to run from the crater
practice.hint: Think about the food chain step in the lab. What does a plant-eater need?
practice.explain: Without sunlight, plants could not make food. Big plant-eaters like Triceratops starved, and the meat-eaters that hunted them starved next.

pool.prompt: About how long ago did the K-Pg extinction happen?
pool.hint: The clay layer and the Chicxulub crater are the same age. What was it?
pool.explain: It happened about 66 million years ago, at the end of the Cretaceous period, long before any humans lived.

pool.prompt: Which metal in the thin clay layer was the first big clue to an asteroid?
pool.hint: Which metal is rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids?
pool.explain: Iridium. The Alvarez team found about 30 times more of it in the clay than in the rock around it.

choices: Under the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico
pool.hint: In the lab, which crater was 66 million years old and 180 km wide?
pool.explain: Chicxulub is buried under the Yucatán Peninsula and the sea floor next to it, in Mexico.

pool.prompt: Which of these groups is still alive today?
pool.hint: Which group of dinosaurs did not die out?
pool.explain: Birds are dinosaurs that survived. Pterosaurs and ammonites died out completely.

pool.prompt: Put these in order: A plants die back, B the Sun is blocked, C plant-eaters starve. Which order is right?
pool.hint: Plants need light. Plant-eaters need plants.
pool.explain: The Sun is blocked, then plants die back, then the animals that eat plants starve.

pool.prompt: Sam says the asteroid killed every living thing. What is wrong?
choices: About a quarter of kinds of living things survived, such as birds and small mammals
pool.hint: If everything died, where would today's animals come from?
pool.explain: About three quarters of species died out. The rest, including birds, frogs, turtles and small mammals, lived on.

pool.prompt: Which animal had the best chance of surviving the dark, cold years after the impact?
choices: A small burrowing mammal that ate insects and seeds
A huge plant-eater that ate fresh leaves
A big meat-eater that hunted plant-eaters
pool.hint: Which food lasted when plants stopped growing? Where could an animal shelter?
pool.explain: Small animals need little food, seeds and insects lasted in the dark, and burrows gave shelter. Big animals ran out of food.

pool.prompt: In a cliff, which rock layer formed first?
pool.hint: Each new layer settles on top of the ones already there.
pool.explain: Layers build up from the bottom, so the bottom layer formed first and is the oldest.

pool.prompt: The asteroid was about 10 km wide. A school bus is about 10 metres long, and 1 km is 1,000 metres. How many buses end to end would match {k} km?
pool.hint: 1 km = 1,000 m, so 100 buses of 10 m fit in 1 km. Multiply {k} by 100.
pool.explain: {k} × 100 = {=k*100} buses. Ten km, the width of the asteroid, is 1,000 buses.

pool.prompt: For every 1 kind of living thing that survived, about 3 kinds died out. In a group where {n} kinds survived, about how many kinds died out?
pool.hint: Three died out for every one that lived. Work out 3 × {n}.
pool.explain: 3 × {n} = {=3*n} kinds died out. That is the three quarters that went extinct.
